question: Local anaesthetics produce reversible nerve blockade primarily by which mechanism?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Potassium channels are not the primary target. Local anaesthetics act on sodium channels.

answers.text: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potential propagation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Local anaesthetics bind to voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the inactivated state, preventing depolarisation and nerve conduction.
GABA-A agonism is the mechanism of benzodiazepines and barbiturates, not local anaesthetics.
COX inhibition is the mechanism of NSAIDs. Local anaesthetics act on sodium channels.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pharmacology section: local anaesthetics bind voltage-gated sodium channels, not potassium channels or GABA receptors.
Well done. Na⁺ channel blockade is the universal mechanism — understanding this explains differential blockade, dose-response, and toxicity.
